title: R = 1.5 is not 50% more
hook: Each case passes it to 1.5 others. After a month, is that 50% more cases, or far more?

knows: R is the average number of people one case infects
doesNotKnow: that R is growth per generation of infection, so it compounds
that R below 1 shrinks an outbreak the same compounding way

misconception: R = 1.5 means cases grow by 50% over the whole outbreak.
objective: The learner can explain that R multiplies new cases once per generation, so 20 cases at R = 1.5 become about 228 after 6 generations, and that R below 1 makes each generation smaller.

claims.text: Starting from 20 new cases with R = 1.5 per generation, the generations have about 20, 30, 45, 68, 101, 152 and 228 new cases; 20 x 1.5^6 = 227.8.
claims.source: Arithmetic; computed in Demo.tsx (cases) and in node (artifacts/scratch/w3life/check.mjs).

claims.text: On the stage, R = 0.8 gives 20 x 0.8^6 = 5.2 new cases in generation 6, R = 1.2 gives 59.7, and R = 2 gives 1,280; below 1 each generation is smaller than the last.
claims.source: Arithmetic (node); same function draws the stage.

claims.text: The model is a made-up infection with R fixed, generations exactly 5 days apart and no overlap between generations.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; stated in the question and on the stage ('Toy: R fixed, generations 5 days apart').

claims.text: In real outbreaks R changes as behaviour and immunity change.
claims.source: Anderson R.M. & May R.M. (1991) Infectious Diseases of Humans: Dynamics and Control, Oxford UP, ch. 2 and 4.

recall.question: A made-up outbreak has R = 2 and 10 new cases in one generation. With R unchanged, about how many new cases are in the third generation after it?
recall.why: R multiplies once per generation: 10 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 80.
